title: Dating an embryo

objective.text: Explain how an embryo's age is counted in days and Carnegie stages.

body.general: How old is an embryo on 'day 16'? Embryology counts days from fertilization [f1]. Doctors count a pregnancy from the last period, about two weeks earlier, so week 3 here is about week 5 of pregnancy [f2]. Carnegie stages sort embryos by shape, not age, so one stage covers a few days [f1]. Stage 6, when the three body layers start to form (gastrulation), is days 14–15 [f3]. Sources disagree on stage ages, so this app always shows the book's day [f4].
body.mbbs: Langman dates embryos in days after fertilization [f1]. Clinical (gestational) age counts from the last menstrual period, about two weeks earlier, so developmental week 3 is about gestational week 5 [f2]. That is often before the pregnancy is known [f2]. Carnegie stages group embryos by external form, not age or length, so each stage spans several days [f1]. Gastrulation begins at stage 6 (days 14–15) [f3]. Stage ages are estimates, so on screen we give the book's day [f4]. Birth comes about 38 weeks after fertilization, which is 40 gestational weeks [f6].

facts.text: The book dates embryos in days after fertilization; Carnegie stages group embryos by their form, so a stage spans a few days.
Week 3 after fertilization is about gestational week 5, counted from the last menstrual period, often before a pregnancy is known.
Carnegie stage 6 (days 14–15) shows the first primitive streak, the start of gastrulation; stage 7 is days 16–18.
On screen we give the book's day for each event; stage ages from other sources are estimates.
⚑ Newer evidence (D-030, D-039): one stage table runs older than the classic ages at stages 6–13, and equal or younger later.
Birth comes about 266 days (38 weeks) after fertilization, or about 280 days (40 weeks) after the last menstrual period.

misconceptions.wrong: Gestational age and fertilization age are the same number.
misconceptions.right: Gestational age counts from the last menstrual period, about two weeks before fertilization.

misconceptions.wrong: A Carnegie stage is a fixed age in days.
misconceptions.right: A stage is set by the embryo's form, so each stage spans a few days.

checks.prompt: A pregnancy is 5 weeks from the last period. About how many weeks since fertilization?
checks.why: Gestational age starts about two weeks before fertilization, so 5 gestational weeks is about week 3 of development.

checks.prompt: What decides an embryo's Carnegie stage?
checks.why: Stages are defined by features; ages and lengths are only estimates for each stage.

checks.prompt: Gastrulation starts at Carnegie stage 6. Which days does the book give for it?
checks.why: The book's table puts the first streak at days 14–15, which is stage 6.

adult: The same two-week gap explains due dates: about 38 weeks of development is counted as 40 weeks of pregnancy [f6].

remember.q: Embryology counts days from what event?
Week 3 of development is about which week of pregnancy?
remember.a: About gestational week 5, counted from the last period [f2].
The embryo's form, not its age [f1].
